The licensure guide, without the maze.

What you need to work in another state, how long it tends to take, and the documents to keep ready.

Start with where you are licensed now

Your license is issued by a state, and that state's rules decide where you can practice. Before you look at assignments, check two things: which state issued your license, and whether it is a single-state or a multistate license.

Compact licenses

Nurses whose primary residence is in a state that belongs to the Nurse Licensure Compact can hold one multistate license and practice in the other compact states without applying again. If you qualify, a large part of the country is open to you from day one.

Several other professions, physical therapy among them, have their own interstate compacts. The rules differ by profession, so ask your recruiter what applies to yours.

Single-state licenses

If the state you want is outside your compact, or your profession has none, you apply to that state's board for a license by endorsement. Expect to provide:

  • Verification of your current license and any others you have held
  • Transcripts or proof of education
  • Fingerprints and a background check
  • The application fee, and sometimes a jurisprudence exam

How long it takes

Timelines vary widely. Some boards issue a temporary license in days; others take several weeks or longer, especially around graduation season. Apply as soon as you know which state you want, and do not book travel until the license is in hand or your recruiter has confirmed the timeline.

Certifications and other requirements

Facilities set their own requirements on top of the state's. BLS is close to universal. ACLS, PALS, NRP or a specialty certification depends on the unit. School and correctional settings often add an education credential or a security clearance.

Keep these ready

  • License numbers and expiry dates for every state you hold
  • Current certification cards
  • Immunization records and a recent TB test
  • Two professional references who have supervised you recently
  • An up-to-date résumé with exact dates and unit types

Board rules change. Always confirm the current requirements with the state board itself; your recruiter will point you to the right page.
